strengths: The paper provides a coherent and mathematically careful application of modern e-value/sequential testing machinery (Ville's inequality, mixture martingales, Wald-style identities, e-BH) to the problem of monitoring equilibrium play, and the proofs in the appendices appear internally consistent and correctly executed.

The framework is presented in a unified way across several equilibrium notions (Nash, correlated, coarse correlated, approximate equilibria) and is extended from static repeated games to stochastic games via a likelihood-ratio construction, which is a reasonable generalization of Wald's SPRT idea to state-dependent dynamics.

Detection-time bounds are derived under the alternative (Theorem 2.7, 3.4) and the paper attempts to connect empirical detection times to the theoretical O(1/eta^2) and O(1/KL) scaling laws through synthetic experiments (Figures 2, 3, 7).

The FDR extension via e-BH is a sensible addition that in principle increases power relative to a conservative FWER procedure, and the nestedness/validity properties (Theorem 2.8, Proposition 2.9) are proven.
weaknesses: The core normal-form framework requires observing the full counterfactual payoff u_i(a'_i, a_{-i}) for every possible unilateral deviation a'_i at every round, not just the realized payoff. This is an extremely strong informational assumption that is rarely satisfiable in real multi-agent systems (e.g., trading, autonomous driving, the very applications cited in the introduction), which substantially undercuts the paper's claimed motivation of "real-time" monitoring in practical multi-agent deployments.

The stochastic-game extension (Section 3) requires the monitor to already know the full candidate equilibrium policy pi (and, for detection, the specific or mixture-of alternative policies) in closed form to compute likelihood ratios. Combined with the normal-form requirement above, neither of the two settings actually relaxes both of the unrealistic assumptions (knowledge of the equilibrium strategy, and/or access to all counterfactual payoffs) simultaneously; the discussion section admits this gap but treats it as a minor "future work" item rather than a central limitation of the contribution's practical relevance.

No empirical or even careful qualitative comparison is made against the most directly relevant prior baseline, Babichenko et al. (2017), despite extensive textual claims of improving on it (e.g., "linear rather than super-exponential" bounds, faster detection). The linear-vs-super-exponential improvement claimed in the introduction and Appendix D is asserted rather than explicitly derived or empirically demonstrated. This leaves the central significance claim (that this method is a meaningful advance over existing equilibrium-testing approaches) largely unsubstantiated.

All experiments are small, hand-constructed synthetic environments (a 2x2 normal-form game, a 5x4 grid-soccer game, a 10x10 predator-prey game) with engineered, often weak or arbitrary deviation signals. There is no real-world dataset, no comparison to alternative sequential/changepoint detectors (e.g., CUSUM, Shiryaev-Roberts, or naive fixed-window retesting, all of which are discussed in related work but never benchmarked), and no evaluation of statistical power/robustness under model misspecification or noisy/estimated payoffs.

Several key theoretical novelties are mostly adaptations of very recent, essentially off-the-shelf techniques (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas coin-betting e-values, Robbins mixture e-values, Tavyrikov et al. e-BH), applied in a fairly mechanical way to the equilibrium-testing setting; the genuinely new technical content (e.g., the stochastic-game extension, Theorem 3.4) is incremental relative to standard SPRT/Wald-identity arguments, limiting the paper's originality beyond its application framing.

The practical workflow for choosing the mixture distribution, thresholds, and weights in the e-BH procedure, and the sensitivity of results to the (unrealistic) "Dirac-mixture" and smoothing/support assumptions used in the stochastic-game experiments (e.g., the artificial support-smoothing fix with beta=0.05 needed to avoid infinite likelihood ratios), are not well justified as something a practitioner could set without extensive problem-specific tuning, undermining the claimed ease of deployment.

strengths: The paper builds a technically rigorous, well-grounded sequential testing framework for equilibrium monitoring, rooted in the e-value/safe-anytime-valid-inference literature (Ville's inequality, mixture martingales, e-BH), with complete and careful proofs provided in the appendix for all main claims (Lemmas 2.2-2.3, Theorems 2.6-2.9, 3.3-3.4).

The work fills a genuine gap relative to prior fixed-sample equilibrium testing (e.g., Babichenko et al. 2017) by offering an online, anytime-valid procedure that does not require a pre-specified sample size, and that requires weaker informational assumptions (no need to know the candidate equilibrium strategy in the normal-form setting).

The extension from FWER to FDR control via an e-BH-style procedure is theoretically justified (Theorem 2.8) and is shown to provably detect no later than the FWER procedure (Proposition 2.9), giving a principled power improvement for large games.

The extension to stochastic games (Section 3) generalizes Wald's SPRT/likelihood-ratio approach to state-dependent Markovian dynamics, with finite-time detection-time bounds tied to KL divergence (Theorem 3.4) and a mixture extension for unknown deviation magnitude (Remark 3.5, Appendix F.5).

The paper is unusually thorough in its supplementary material: it treats alternative equilibrium concepts (correlated, coarse correlated, approximate Nash; Appendix D), motivates the necessity of a slack parameter η with a concrete worked example (Appendix E), provides an alternative informational setting (Appendix G), and conducts fairly extensive empirical validation of theoretical scaling laws (e.g., O(1/ε²) detection-time scaling confirmed in grid-soccer and predator-prey experiments, Figures 2-3), plus parameter sensitivity analyses (Table 1, Figures 6-7) and sanity checks of the log-optimal betting fraction (Appendix H.1.4).
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation, while theoretically well-aligned, remains limited to small, synthetic environments (a single 2x2 normal-form game, small gridworld stochastic games); there is no evaluation on larger-scale multi-agent systems, real learning dynamics (e.g., actual no-regret/MARL learners drifting from equilibrium, as motivated in the introduction), or comparison against alternative change-detection baselines (CUSUM, Shiryaev-Roberts, or the offline Babichenko et al. test), making it hard to assess practical advantage beyond the toy settings studied.

The normal-form framework requires access to exact counterfactual payoff evaluations u_i(a'_i, a_{-i}) for all players and all alternative actions at every round, which is a strong and often unrealistic assumption in real systems (one typically cannot observe payoffs for actions not taken); this limitation is acknowledged but not mitigated.

The stochastic-game extension (Section 3) requires exact knowledge of the candidate equilibrium policy π (and alternative π^(1)) as explicit probability distributions to compute likelihood ratios — a considerably stronger requirement than the normal-form case, and one that conflicts somewhat with the motivating real-world examples (automated trading, autonomous driving) where such policies are typically not directly observable; the authors flag this as an open problem but do not address it.

The mixture-based robustification over λ or over deviation strategies π^(1) requires specifying or discretizing a prior over a potentially high-dimensional space of alternatives; while workable in the paper's low-dimensional experiments (grid search over a handful of ε/λ values), it is unclear how this would scale to larger action/state spaces or more complex deviation classes.

The main text's empirical section is brief (about one page) with most substantive results deferred to a lengthy appendix; while the appendix is thorough, the core paper would benefit from a more self-contained demonstration of practical utility, e.g., in a more realistic or higher-dimensional multi-agent setting.

strengths: Rigorous and complete theoretical development: e-value/supermartingale constructions, Ville's inequality-based FWER control, Kelly-optimal betting analysis, mixture martingales for unknown deviation magnitude, and e-BH-based FDR control are all proven carefully, with full proofs deferred to a very thorough appendix.

Clear, well-motivated improvements over the closest prior work (Babichenko et al., 2017): the method is sequential/anytime rather than requiring a fixed sample size, does not require knowledge of the equilibrium strategy itself (only counterfactual payoffs), and yields sharper (linear rather than super-exponential) bounds for correlated equilibrium testing.

Nice unification across equilibrium concepts (Nash, correlated, coarse correlated, approximate) and a genuine extension from static normal-form games to stochastic games via a likelihood-ratio SPRT-type construction, including KL-divergence-based detection-time bounds and an ergodicity-based analysis.

The FDR extension via e-BH is a valuable practical contribution for large games, with a clean theoretical guarantee (Theorem 2.8) and a provable ordering result (Proposition 2.9) showing FDR control is never slower than FWER control.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: they empirically validate FWER control, demonstrate FDR speedup with sample-level scatter plots, verify the predicted O(1/ε²) scaling law in a stochastic game, and test robustness to unknown deviation magnitude via the mixture approach; a larger-scale (n=20, m=60 hypotheses) population game experiment in the appendix supports scalability of the qualitative findings.

Honest treatment of limitations (counterfactual payoff access, requiring knowledge of target policy in stochastic games) and inclusion of a concrete counterexample (Appendix E) justifying the necessity of the slack parameter η.
weaknesses: The core statistical toolkit (e-values, coin-betting constructions, Ville's inequality, mixture martingales, e-BH for FDR) is largely adapted from existing sequential testing / safe anytime-valid inference literature (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, Wang & Ramdas, Robbins, etc.); the paper's novelty lies primarily in the application to game-theoretic equilibrium monitoring rather than in fundamentally new statistical machinery, which somewhat limits the technical originality relative to the statistics literature it builds on.

There is a conceptual tension between the paper's motivating narrative (learning agents whose behavior gradually or abruptly drifts away from equilibrium over time due to updating objectives/adapting strategies) and the actual technical model, which assumes the joint action profile is drawn i.i.d. from a *fixed* (possibly unknown) distribution at every round under both H0 and H1; this does not naturally capture continuously evolving/non-stationary learning dynamics, and the paper does not clearly reconcile this gap.

The requirement of observing counterfactual payoff evaluations ui(a'_i, a_-i) for every possible deviation in the normal-form setting, and of knowing the target policy π in the stochastic-game setting, are significant practical restrictions; while acknowledged as limitations and future work, no concrete methodology (e.g., value-function estimation) is offered to bridge this gap, limiting immediate real-world applicability.

All experiments are on synthetic, relatively small or moderate-scale simulated environments (2×2 games, 5×4 grid soccer, 10×10 predator-prey, a 20-player RPS population game); there is no real-world or naturally occurring multi-agent dataset used to validate the framework's practical utility, e.g., in economic, trading, or LLM-agent settings mentioned as motivating applications.

The data-splitting/screening baseline introduced in Appendix H.2 to reduce multiple-testing burden is argued informally (via independence of screening/testing windows) rather than being fully integrated into the paper's formal theoretical framework, leaving a slight gap between the appendix experiments and the core theory.

Presentation is extremely dense, with substantial material (including most novel technical content beyond Section 2's core results) relegated to a very long appendix; the main text alone may leave readers without a full picture of the contribution's scope and rigor.

strengths: The paper builds on solid theoretical foundations (e-values, supermartingales, Ville's inequality, optional stopping) and the proofs provided in the appendices appear technically correct and carefully worked through.

The extension of Babichenko et al. (2017)'s fixed-sample equilibrium testing to an anytime-valid sequential setting is a sensible and well-motivated generalization, and the unification across Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria in a single framework is a nice organizational contribution.

The integration of e-BH-style FDR control into the sequential testing procedure, with a theorem showing FDR-based detection is never slower than FWER-based detection (Proposition 2.9), is a clean and useful practical refinement for large games.

The extension to stochastic games via likelihood-ratio martingales, with KL-divergence-based detection-time bounds tied to the stationary distribution of the alternative policy, is a reasonable generalization of Wald's SPRT to Markovian settings.

The experimental section, while synthetic, does empirically validate the key theoretical claims (FWER control, FDR speedup, O(1/epsilon^2) detection-time scaling, robustness of the mixture martingale to unknown deviation magnitude), and a larger-scale population game experiment in the appendix helps show that conclusions are not an artifact of the minimal 2x2 example.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is largely a careful but fairly direct application of existing betting/e-value machinery (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas betting e-values, Robbins-style mixtures, Kelly criterion, e-BH) to a new problem domain, rather than a fundamentally new statistical technique; the novelty is primarily in the combination and the game-theoretic framing rather than in the underlying statistical tools.

The normal-form framework requires observing counterfactual payoffs ui(a'_i, a-i) for all untaken actions at every round, which is a strong and often unrealistic assumption in real multi-agent deployments (the paper itself concedes this would require 'a model of the environment'), undermining the practical motivation given in the introduction (detecting collusion, verifying rational play, etc.).

The stochastic-game extension requires full knowledge of the candidate target policy π to compute exact likelihoods, as well as ergodicity of the alternative policy's induced chain and a stationarity-at-start assumption for the sharp detection-time bound (Theorem 3.4) — conditions that are unlikely to hold exactly in the motivating applications (autonomous driving, automated trading) mentioned in the introduction.

All experiments are small, fully synthetic toy environments (a hand-engineered 2x2 game, small gridworld soccer, gridworld predator-prey) with no real-world or even moderately realistic multi-agent data; there is no comparison against natural baselines (e.g., naive repeated application of offline tests, classical change-point detectors such as CUSUM/Shiryaev-Roberts mentioned in related work) to demonstrate concrete practical advantage.

The alternative hypothesis depends on a fixed slack parameter η that must be specified in advance, and the paper's own appendix analysis shows that the 'optimal' λ=η choice is actually suboptimal/overly conservative for realistic game instances, raising questions about how a practitioner would choose η or λ in practice without already knowing the deviation magnitude.

Much of the technical substance (all proofs, most theorem statements' practical implications, large portions of experimental detail) is relegated to a very long appendix, making the main paper somewhat thin on self-contained verifiable content and harder to assess without extensive cross-referencing.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: moving equilibrium testing in games from the classical fixed-sample-size offline setting (e.g., Babichenko et al., 2017) to an anytime-valid, sequential monitoring setting, which is practically important since real multi-agent systems are observed online and standard re-testing on growing data is a form of 'sequential p-hacking' as the authors note.

Technically rigorous: the e-value/supermartingale construction (Lemma 2.2-2.3), the Ville's inequality-based FWER control (Theorem 2.6), the Kelly-optimal betting analysis (Prop 2.4), and the mixture-based detection time bounds (Theorem 2.7) are all carefully derived, with complete proofs provided in the appendix.

Meaningful extensions beyond the basic framework: unification across Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria (Appendix D) with an improved bound for correlated equilibrium that is linear rather than super-exponential in the number of actions; integration of e-BH for FDR control with provable power gains over FWER control (Proposition 2.9); and a non-trivial generalization to stochastic games via likelihood-ratio martingales connected to Wald's SPRT and KL-divergence-based detection time bounds under ergodicity (Theorem 3.4).

The method requires weaker informational assumptions than prior work (no need to know the equilibrium strategy π itself, only payoff evaluations for deviations), which is explicitly and correctly compared against Babichenko et al. (2017).

Experiments, although synthetic, directly validate the core theoretical claims: FWER/FDR control under the null, the FDR speedup over FWER (confirmed empirically in both a small 2x2 game and a larger 60-hypothesis Rock-Paper-Scissors population game), and the predicted O(1/ε^2) scaling law for detection time in stochastic games, including a demonstration of robustness when the deviation magnitude is unknown via the mixture approach.

Extensive and transparent appendices, including full proofs, sensitivity analyses (over α, λ, η), additional scaled-up experiments, and detailed gameplay visualizations that aid reproducibility and build confidence in the empirical claims.
weaknesses: Both branches of the framework rely on fairly strong informational assumptions that are acknowledged but not resolved: the normal-form test requires access to counterfactual payoff evaluations for all possible deviations (not just realized payoffs), and the stochastic-game test requires exact knowledge of the candidate policy's action probabilities to compute likelihood ratios; in many realistic multi-agent monitoring settings (e.g., observing external agents) neither may be available.

The i.i.d. sampling assumption for action profiles in the normal-form setting (Section 2) is a significant simplification relative to the motivating scenario of agents that are continuously learning and potentially drifting; temporally dependent or non-stationary play (which is precisely what one might expect from 'drifting' learning agents) is not covered by the main theoretical guarantees.

The alternative hypothesis is defined only as an η-approximate equilibrium with a fixed slack parameter, which, while technically necessary (as shown in Appendix E), restricts the scope of detectable deviations and leaves open how to choose η in practice without strong power loss (as the λ=η optimality discussion itself shows is data/instance-dependent).

All experiments are small-scale, synthetic benchmarks (toy matrix games, gridworld soccer, gridworld predator-prey); there is no evaluation on real or semi-real multi-agent data, nor empirical comparison against alternative baselines such as the original Babichenko et al. fixed-sample test or classical sequential change-point methods (CUSUM/Shiryaev-Roberts), which would better substantiate practical significance beyond confirming the paper's own theory.

The stochastic-game detection-time guarantee (Theorem 3.4) assumes the chain is started in stationarity and is ergodic; the treatment of the more realistic non-stationary start/burn-in case is only sketched qualitatively rather than formally bounded.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential misuse or consequences of real-time strategic-deviation detection (e.g., surveillance, enforcement actions against agents mistakenly flagged).
